extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century literate public (interested in literature, morals, and social customs)
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance and commentary about what constitutes a 'great genius', the balance of natural talent and art, social customs (country wakes), steadiness of character, and methods of consolation in affliction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great natural genius (first class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those few who, by the mere strength of natural parts and without assistance of arts or learning, produce works that delight their times and astonish posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such geniuses are 'nobly wild and extravagant' and achieve sublimity beyond polished art, but often 'failed in, or... were very much above the Nicety and Correctness of the Moderns.' Examples cited: Homer, some Eastern writers, Pindar. Anti-pattern: judging these writers only by modern niceties and laughing at indecencies without relishing the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe bienséance/decency in similes and allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern practice (especially in 'colder Regions') values a scrupulous nicety and exactness in comparisons and allusions — the French 'bienséance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ancient writers sometimes use bold or indecent comparisons (e.g., Solomon's similes, Homeric analogies), later writers should be attentive to appropriateness of comparison. The rule of decency in allusion is presented as a corrective development, not an absolute aesthetic negation of ancient force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trained/disciplined genius (second class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geniuses who have formed themselves by rules and submitted natural talents to the corrections and restraints of art (e.g., Plato, Aristotle, Virgil, Tully, Milton, Sir Francis Bacon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their greatness manifests differently — like a rich soil laid out in ordered gardens. This discipline can refine power into structured excellence. Scoring note: greatness in this class is equal in magnitude but different in manner from raw genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of excessive imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk that disciplined geniuses may cramp their abilities by forming entirely upon models and losing their peculiar voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation of the best authors should not replace originality: 'An Imitation of the best Authors is not to compare with a good Original.' Anti-pattern: following 'Irregularities by Rule' or using 'little Tricks of Art' to strain after unbounded flights of nature, producing mere distortion without divine impulse (e.g., modern Pindaricks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of original, peculiar manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few writers make an extraordinary figure who do not have something peculiar wholly their own in thought or expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages authors to retain distinctive mental or stylistic traits rather than subsuming themselves to models; originality is a decisive advantage over mere polished imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wasted genius: misapplication to trifles
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark that great talent is sometimes 'thrown away upon Trifles'—skill and perseverance applied to trivial pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative anecdote: a shepherd perfecting juggling eggs to an extraordinary degree but thereby developing a solemnness better suited to mathematical pursuit (Archimedes). Implicit prescription: apply assiduity to worthy ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country wakes promote courtship and display of vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Country wakes (eve-feasts of church dedications) assemble all ages and sexes, providing occasions where people show their skills and recommend themselves to one another, often leading to love and marriages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive assessment: such festivals encourage bodily exercises (wrestling, cudgel-play, football), emulation, and opportunities for young people to display fitness and win mates. Prescriptive note: this public display is socially useful and aligns with ancient practices (Greek agápai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel popular emulation into civic improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of emulation evident in wakes could be directed toward improving handicraft trades by setting annual prizes for excellence in arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical proposal: replace mere sport-prizes with awards that promote apprenticeships and craftsmanship; links popular competitive energy to national benefit (analogy to ancient pentathlon prizes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical exercise as civic virtue (long bow statute example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical note that an old statute obliges certain men to keep and exercise the long bow, which maintained national martial readiness without a standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit criterion: encouraging regular physical exercises among the populace yields public advantage and readiness for defense; exercises at wakes contribute to health and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy/steadfastness as a moral and social virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconstancy, especially regarding religion or party, makes a person contemptible; steadiness in great articles of life makes one respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: before changing important allegiances (religion, politics), ensure conviction is strong and not motivated by worldly advantage. Practical prescription: adhere steadfastly to one great end to avoid irresolution and misery; scoring note: steadiness trumps fashionable variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irresolution by selecting one chief aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Irresolution among competing schemes (ambition, interest, inclination, reason) is a universal cause of disquiet; better to choose a way of life and adhere even if imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set one ultimate aim (e.g., live by dictates of reason) and treat other goods (wealth, reputation) as secondary when they coincide. Anti-pattern: attempting to be virtuous, wealthy, and popular all at once will lead to 'Misery and Repentance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts of consolation: preferred over speculative rules for happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical skills for supporting oneself under affliction ('arts of consolation') are more necessary than speculative rules for attaining happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive methods for consolation: (1) Read authors who present calamities and human distress (so as to fortify), (2) Associate with sufferers of greater sorrows or virtue, (3) Use comparison to lessen sense of one's woes, (4) Consider that apparent misfortunes may be blessings in a larger view, (5) Religion/devotion often offers comfort. Alternative temperament note: some (St. Evremont) recommend diverting reading (Don Quixote) to stir mirth rather than grave moralists; choose consolatory method according to temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select reading appropriate to consolatory aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Different readers find consolation in different genres: serious moral examples strengthen the mind, while lively humorous works can provide diversion and relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monsieur St. Evremont is cited as preferring authors that stir mirth (e.g., Don Quixote) over Plutarch or Seneca for easing a heavy heart; the essayist suggests preferring moral authors that give instances of calamity to fortify, but acknowledges temperament-specific choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective-taking: compare with greater miseries
rubrics_metrics.description: One method of consolation is to compare personal sorrow with much greater calamities elsewhere to reduce self-pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shipwrecks, deathbed terrors, executions, kingdoms in ashes — by comparison one's private sorrow may diminish. Scoring note: useful for light-to-moderate afflictions; stronger afflictions may require different resources (devotion, fellowship with great sufferers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion/devotion as a primary consolatory resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion and religion naturally attract those in affliction and often provide the deepest consolation; misguided devotion may also console, but sound religion grounded in reason is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist will illustrate by a story to show the power of religion in abating anguish; pragmatic advice: lean on devotions but prefer reasoned religion when possible.
